cards.claim: EMA enables implicit regularization through noise reduction, allowing convergence with higher learning rates than standard SGD without decaying to near-zero
cards.conditions: SGD with momentum (0.9), cosine annealing LR schedule; CIFAR-100 on ResNet-18
cards.effect: Convergence achieved with substantially higher final learning rates while maintaining or improving generalization
cards.evidence: Experimental observation with visualization (Figure 1a-b) showing EMA peaks at epoch 150 with high LR before deteriorating
cards.quote: Averaging during training is an alternative way of to reduce noise in SGD iterates and reach a good solution without too much learning rate decay. This allows to freely tune the final learning rate to control the strength of implicit regularization, while still converging to a good solution within the neighborhood.

cards.claim: EMA can spare the final phase of low learning rate training, reducing compute budget to ~75% of full SGD budget
cards.conditions: Cosine annealing schedule with early stopping; tested on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet
cards.effect: Reduction in training epochs required while maintaining test accuracy
cards.evidence: Experimental observation across multiple datasets and architectures
cards.quote: This suggests that the last phase of SGD training is mostly wasteful, as the iterates are already around a good solution that cannot be accessed (without averaging) because of stochastic noise. In our experiments with cosine annealing, early stopping for EMA was always at of the epochs budget

cards.claim: EMA achieves exceptional performance early in training due to noise reduction, enabling faster learning of general representations
cards.conditions: CIFAR-100 on ResNet-18; training with high learning rates during early epochs
cards.effect: High accuracy achieved in first ~15% of training compared to SGD
cards.evidence: Experimental observation (Figure 1a) showing EMA accuracy trajectory from epoch 0-200
cards.quote: A key difference in the training dynamics of EMA and SGD models is the early-stage performance: EMA models are very effective early in training. Its remarkable performance after just a few epochs partly explains the success of EMA teachers.

cards.claim: EMA improves test accuracy consistently across multiple architectures and datasets
cards.effect: 0.37–1.94 percentage point gains in test accuracy
cards.evidence: Experimental results from Table 1 (mean of 3 runs with confidence intervals)
cards.quote: The EMA model consistently outperforms the baseline in accuracy and loss, and the same is true for SWA. We find that averaging with EMA improves generalization, always outperforming the SGD baseline.

cards.claim: EMA provides magnified robustness to label noise through stronger implicit regularization at higher learning rates
cards.conditions: CIFAR-100N with ~40% label noise; ResNet-34; EMA early-stopped at best accuracy epoch
cards.effect: 65.15% accuracy on CIFAR-100N noise benchmark, competitive with or exceeding specialized robust training methods
cards.evidence: Experimental results from Table 4 and Figure 3 showing EMA peaks at epoch 100 with high LR before memorization occurs
cards.quote: Interestingly, we find that the effect of implicit regularization is magnified in the presence of label noise. The EMA model peaks at accuracy at epoch 100, with a learning rate around, and then decays until it plateaus at at the end of training.

cards.claim: EMA solutions are fundamentally different from SGD solutions, reaching different regions of the loss landscape that generalize better
cards.conditions: General deep learning training with SGD trajectory
cards.effect: Solutions with improved generalization, calibration, prediction consistency, and transfer learning over last-iterate SGD
cards.evidence: Theoretical reasoning combined with experimental validation across multiple metrics
cards.quote: We find that the solutions reached with EMA and early stopping are different from the baseline solution obtained by last-iterate momentum SGD, and conjecture that this is due to implicit regularization via stochastic noise, obtained through the use of larger step-sizes.

cards.claim: Model parameters tolerate larger EMA averaging windows than Batch Norm statistics, but divergence can be recovered by periodic BN stat recomputation
cards.conditions: Models with Batch Normalization (ResNet-18, WideResNet); tested across CIFAR-100 with varying decay rates
cards.effect: With BN recomputation, very large averaging windows (slower decay) improve generalization; without it, divergence occurs
cards.evidence: Experimental observation in Figure 1(b) showing divergence with slow decay that recovers with BN recomputation
cards.quote: As shown in Fig. 1(b), the EMA model can diverge when a very slow decay (i.e., large τ) is used. Interestingly, if we recompute the BN stats of that same EMA model (once after every epoch) we recover full performance, indicating that it is BN that breaks an EMA model as we increase the size of the averaging window.
